instruction: Send a JSON payload to an API endpoint.
context: curl: -d implies POST and sets a form content type, so -H must override it for JSON. Using --data-raw prevents the leading @ in a payload from being read as a filename.

instruction: Post the contents of a JSON file as the request body.
context: curl: an @ prefix on -d reads the body from that file, and @- reads standard input. The @ form strips newlines unless --data-binary is used instead.

instruction: Download a file from a URL that redirects.
context: curl: -L follows redirects, which curl does not do by default, and -f makes it exit non-zero on an HTTP error rather than saving the error page. -o names the output file.

instruction: Check a URL's response headers without downloading the body.
context: curl: capital -I issues a HEAD request and prints only headers, where lowercase -i prints headers plus the body. -sS hides the progress meter but keeps error messages visible.

instruction: Print just the HTTP status code for a health check.
context: curl: -w emits a template after the transfer, with variables like http_code, time_total, and size_download. Discarding the body to /dev/null keeps the output to the single value.

instruction: Call an authenticated endpoint without exposing the token in the process list.
context: curl: -H accepts an @file argument holding header lines, keeping the token out of the command line where ps and shell history would capture it. --netrc-file is the equivalent for basic auth.

instruction: Fetch a URL with automatic retries on transient failures.
context: curl: --retry handles transient errors and timeouts, but by default not HTTP 4xx or 5xx. --retry-all-errors extends it to those, and --max-time bounds the whole operation.

instruction: Stop a request from hanging indefinitely in a script.
context: curl: --connect-timeout bounds only the handshake while --max-time bounds the entire transfer including the body. Setting only the former still allows a slow server to stall forever.

instruction: Test a site on a specific server before DNS is switched over.
context: curl: --resolve pins a hostname and port to an address, so TLS and the Host header still use the real name. This is correct where connecting to the IP directly would break certificate validation.

instruction: Upload a file as multipart form data.
context: curl: -F builds a multipart/form-data body where @ attaches a file and < inserts a file's contents as a plain value. Mixing -F and -d in one request is not allowed.

instruction: Debug a TLS or redirect problem by seeing the full exchange.
context: curl: -v prints request and response headers plus TLS negotiation on stderr, prefixed with > and <. --trace-ascii writes the full body exchange to a file when headers are not enough.

instruction: Keep a session cookie across two requests.
context: curl: -c writes received cookies to a jar file and -b reads them back, so both are needed to maintain a session. Each curl invocation is otherwise stateless.

instruction: Download a documentation site for offline reading.
context: wget: -m enables mirroring, -k rewrites links for local browsing, -E adds html extensions, -p fetches page requisites, and -np stays below the starting directory. This bundle is the standard offline-copy recipe.

instruction: Resume an interrupted large download.
context: wget -c resumes from the existing file's length using a range request, so a partial file is completed rather than restarted. curl spells the same thing -C -.

instruction: Check how ssh will actually connect to a host after config resolution.
context: ssh -G prints the fully resolved configuration for a host and exits without connecting, showing which Host block, user, port, and key would apply. This settles config precedence questions directly.

instruction: Reach a private host by hopping through a bastion.
context: ssh: -J sets a jump host, tunnelling through it without exposing your key to it, which agent forwarding would. It replaces the older ProxyCommand with nc invocation.

instruction: Reach a remote database from a local client through an SSH tunnel.
context: ssh: -L forwards a local port to a host and port reachable from the remote end, where the second host is resolved remotely. -N opens no shell, which suits a tunnel-only session.

instruction: Expose a local development server to a remote machine.
context: ssh: -R is the reverse of -L, opening a listener on the remote side that forwards back to you. The remote listener binds to loopback unless GatewayPorts is enabled in its sshd config.

instruction: Speed up repeated ssh commands to the same host.
context: ssh connection multiplexing reuses one TCP session for later connections, removing the handshake and any second authentication prompt. ControlPersist keeps the master alive after the first session exits.

instruction: Run a single command on a remote host and capture its output.
context: ssh: -n redirects stdin from /dev/null, which stops a remote command from consuming the local script's input inside a loop. Quoting keeps the command from being expanded locally first.

instruction: Generate a modern SSH key pair.
context: ssh-keygen: ed25519 keys are short, fast, and preferred over RSA for new keys. -C sets a comment for identification, and -f names the output file when the default would collide.

instruction: Install my public key on a remote host for passwordless login.
context: ssh-copy-id appends the key to the remote authorized_keys and fixes the directory permissions, which sshd requires to be restrictive. Pass the .pub file, never the private key.

instruction: Copy a directory to a remote host on a non-standard port.
context: scp: capital -P is the port, where ssh uses lowercase -p and scp's -p means preserve timestamps. -r recurses; for anything large or repeated, rsync resumes and scp does not.

instruction: Look up just the IP addresses for a hostname.
context: dig: +short strips everything but the answer values, which is what scripts want. The record type goes last, and +noall +answer is the middle ground that keeps TTLs visible.

instruction: Query a specific DNS server to check propagation.
context: dig: an @ argument selects the server to query, bypassing the system resolver and its cache. This is how to confirm a record has propagated beyond your own network.

instruction: Follow a DNS lookup from the root servers down to find a delegation error.
context: dig +trace performs iterative resolution itself, printing each referral from the root through the TLD to the authoritative server. This is how a broken NS delegation becomes visible.

instruction: Find the hostname associated with an IP address.
context: dig -x builds the in-addr.arpa query for a reverse lookup automatically. A missing PTR record is common and does not indicate the forward record is wrong.

instruction: Check when a site's TLS certificate expires.
context: openssl s_client opens a TLS session and prints the certificate chain. -servername sends SNI, without which a shared host returns its default certificate rather than the one being checked.

instruction: Read the subject and validity dates out of a certificate file.
context: openssl x509: -noout suppresses the re-encoded certificate so only the requested fields print. -text gives the full human-readable dump, and -fingerprint gives the hash used for pinning.

instruction: Confirm a private key matches its certificate.
context: Comparing the modulus hash of the certificate against openssl rsa -noout -modulus for the key proves they pair. A mismatch is the usual cause of a server refusing to start after a renewal.

instruction: Generate a random URL-safe token.
context: openssl rand draws from the cryptographic random source, with -base64 or -hex controlling the encoding. The count is in bytes before encoding, so 32 yields a longer printable string.

instruction: Test whether a TCP port is reachable without sending data.
context: nc: -z scans without sending data, -v reports the result, and -w bounds the wait in seconds. Without -w a filtered port hangs until the system TCP timeout.

instruction: List this machine's IP addresses in a compact form.
context: ip: -brief gives one aligned line per interface instead of the multi-line default, and subcommands abbreviate, so ip a is ip address. -4 or -6 restricts the family.

instruction: Find which interface and gateway traffic to an address will use.
context: ip route get asks the kernel to perform the actual route lookup, rather than making you read the table yourself. It reports the source address chosen too, which matters on multi-homed hosts.

instruction: Check reachability in a script without pinging forever.
context: ping: -c bounds the packet count so the command terminates, and on Linux -W is the per-reply timeout in seconds. ping exits non-zero when no replies arrive, which scripts can test.

instruction: Trace the path to a web server when ICMP is blocked.
context: traceroute: -T uses TCP SYN packets instead of UDP, and -p sets the port, which gets through firewalls that drop the default probes. -n skips reverse DNS for each hop.

instruction: Capture traffic on a port to a file for later analysis.
context: tcpdump: -w writes raw packets for Wireshark rather than printing, -nn skips host and port name resolution, and -s 0 captures full packets. The filter is BPF syntax and must be quoted.

instruction: Read back a capture file and filter it further.
context: tcpdump -r reads a saved capture and applies a new BPF filter, needing no privileges. -A prints payloads as ASCII and -X adds a hex dump alongside.

instruction: Query the Docker daemon API over its Unix socket.
context: curl: --unix-socket connects to a filesystem socket while still speaking HTTP, so the hostname in the URL is ignored but must be present. This is the way to reach daemons with no TCP listener.

instruction: Look up a domain's mail servers quickly.
context: host is the terse alternative to dig, with -t selecting the record type and no flags needed for readable output. dig gives more detail when TTLs or the authority section matter.

instruction: Resolve a hostname exactly the way applications on this machine will.
context: getent queries the full NSS stack, so it honors /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf where dig speaks only to DNS. A disagreement between the two points at a local override.

instruction: Get a summary count of sockets by state.
context: ss -s prints totals per protocol and TCP state without listing individual sockets. A large TIME-WAIT count is normal; a growing CLOSE-WAIT count indicates an application not closing descriptors.

instruction: Sync to a host whose SSH runs on a non-standard port.
context: rsync: -e replaces the remote shell command entirely, which is where ssh options belong since rsync has no port flag of its own. -z compresses in transit, worth it on slow links only.

instruction: Download several URLs concurrently in one command.
context: curl: --parallel transfers multiple URLs at once and --parallel-max caps the concurrency. Capital -O derives each filename from its URL, and one -O is needed per URL.

instruction: List listening sockets on macOS.
context: macOS ships netstat rather than ss, and its -p selects a protocol where Linux netstat -p means show the process. Use lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN when process attribution is needed.

instruction: Bound a reachability check on macOS.
context: BSD ping spells the overall deadline -t in seconds, while on Linux -t is the IP time-to-live and -W is the reply timeout. This flag means different things on each platform.

instruction: List network interface addresses on macOS.
context: macOS has no ip command; ifconfig remains the interface tool and networksetup handles service-level configuration. route get replaces ip route get for path lookups.

instruction: Resolve a hostname on macOS bypassing the system cache.
context: dig ships with macOS and speaks straight to DNS, skipping the mDNSResponder cache that ping and browsers use. dscacheutil -q host reflects the cached view instead.
